Bolivia's constitution of 2009 renamed the country the Plurinational State of Bolivia and recognised its Indigenous nations and 36 Indigenous languages as official alongside Spanish. Voters approved it in a referendum on 25 January 2009, and President Evo Morales, an Aymara and the country's first Indigenous president, put it into force on 7 February.

Most Bolivians are of Indigenous descent, above all Quechua and Aymara, yet since Spanish rule power had sat with a Spanish speaking elite. The new constitution:

  • gave Indigenous communities rights to self government and a voice over land and natural resources
  • made the state the owner of gas and minerals
  • capped new landholdings at 5,000 hectares
  • recognised the coca leaf as part of Andean heritage

It capped years of protest that began with the gas conflict of 2003 and brought Morales to power in the election of 2005. It is Bolivia's seventeenth constitution. Its limit of two terms in a row was later at the centre of the crisis of 2019, when Morales ran for a fourth term and was forced out. Ecuador had adopted a similar plurinational constitution in 2008.
